power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Why do we touch ourselves? A Hypothesis on How We Maintain the Bodily Self

author.affiliation:

								Linköping University

text.text: Why do we keep touching ourselves?

Here, I propose the hypothesis that recurrent selfgenerated sensations may contribute to maintaining embodied self-experience by providing reliable evidence about the body as a source of action and sensation.
Self-touch generates predictable sensory consequences of one's own actions, thereby potentially reinforcing bodily agency, ownership, self-location, and self-other-distinction.
Within this account, sensory attenuation follows from successful prediction.

Social touch extends this process beyond the individual, as sensory and affective signals are regulated between interacting bodies, highlighting the relational character of self-other-differentiation.

The framework predicts that destabilizing bodily self-experience should increase self-evidence-generating behaviors, that reliable selfgenerated feedback should accelerate recovery, and that disrupting action-sensory contingency should abolish this benefit.
Autism and schizophrenia illustrate how altered sensory and social conditions may interact with such self-maintenance processes.
During the covid pandemic, we humans became suddenly aware of the frequency at which we touch our own face.
In fact, a study found it was around 50 times per hour (Rahman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In fact, a study found it was around 50 times per hour <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Rahman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: But as an energy-preserving species, why do we keep touching ourselves?
For some touches, it is easy to find a reason: we rub a painful spot, scratch an itch, or remove hair from the face (Zhang et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For some touches, it is easy to find a reason: we rub a painful spot, scratch an itch, or remove hair from the face <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Zhang et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, most of our self-directed touches go unnoticed to our own conscious awareness.

Self-directed actions are not confined to grooming or responding to irritation: self-touch is frequent in everyday life, begins early in development (Castiello et al., 2010; DiMercurio et al., 2018), and occurs in both solitary and social situations.
text.formatted: Self-directed actions are not confined to grooming or responding to irritation: self-touch is frequent in everyday life, begins early in development <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Castiello et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">DiMercurio et al., 2018)</ref>, and occurs in both solitary and social situations.

text.text: Infants use self-touch in self-soothing (Moszkowski & Stack, 2007), and also increase it in response to positive social stimulation (Filippa et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Infants use self-touch in self-soothing <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Moszkowski & Stack, 2007)</ref>, and also increase it in response to positive social stimulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Filippa et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In adults, facial self-touch becomes more frequent during stress, nervousness, and cognitive demand (Grunwald et al., 2014; Mueller et al., 2019; Spille et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In adults, facial self-touch becomes more frequent during stress, nervousness, and cognitive demand <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Grunwald et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Mueller et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Spille et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These observations raise a question that is easily overlooked when self-touch is treated primarily as a sensory consequence to be filtered out: what does touching oneself accomplish for the organism?
Self-touch encompasses behaviors with different, potentially overlapping functions.
Rubbing, stroking, squeezing, and scratching should not be assumed to have the same sensory or regulatory effects.

Alongside pain modulation and itch relief (Kammers et al., 2010), proposed functions include regulating arousal, directing attention towards the body, and supporting emotional and cognitive regulation (Dreisoerner et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Alongside pain modulation and itch relief <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Kammers et al., 2010)</ref>, proposed functions include regulating arousal, directing attention towards the body, and supporting emotional and cognitive regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Dreisoerner et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: During a working-memory task, spontaneous facial self-touch occurred particularly during distraction, suggesting a possible role in refocusing attention (Mueller et al., 2019).
text.formatted: During a working-memory task, spontaneous facial self-touch occurred particularly during distraction, suggesting a possible role in refocusing attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Mueller et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Self-touch in social interactions may additionally serve communicative functions (Harrigan, 1985; Streeck, 2020).
text.formatted: Self-touch in social interactions may additionally serve communicative functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Harrigan, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Streeck, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Its significance therefore depends on the form of contact and the context in which it occurs; neither its frequency nor its association with stress establishes a single underlying mechanism.

In experimental tasks, self-generated tactile stimuli are commonly perceived as less intense or less ticklish than externally generated stimuli (Sarah-Jayne Blakemore et al., 2000; Kilteni et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In experimental tasks, self-generated tactile stimuli are commonly perceived as less intense or less ticklish than externally generated stimuli (Sarah-Jayne <ref type="bibr">Blakemore et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Kilteni et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The classical explanation invokes an efference copy of the motor command, which allows the sensory consequences of an action to be predicted and attenuated (Von Helmholtz, 1867).
text.formatted: The classical explanation invokes an efference copy of the motor command, which allows the sensory consequences of an action to be predicted and attenuated <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">(Von Helmholtz, 1867)</ref>.

text.text: Human studies implicate interactions between the cerebellum and somatosensory cortex, with the supplementary motor area proposed as a source of the efferent signal (Kilteni et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Human studies implicate interactions between the cerebellum and somatosensory cortex, with the supplementary motor area proposed as a source of the efferent signal <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Kilteni et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This attenuation is not fixed: introducing a delay between action and touch can reduce it, whereas repeated exposure can produce adaptation to the delay (Fritz & Zimmermann, 2023; Kilteni & Ehrsson, 2024).
text.formatted: This attenuation is not fixed: introducing a delay between action and touch can reduce it, whereas repeated exposure can produce adaptation to the delay <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Fritz & Zimmermann, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Kilteni & Ehrsson, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Illusory self-touch produces comparable attenuation (Pyasik et al., 2021), as does the self-touch of an embodied prosthesis (Fritsch et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Illusory self-touch produces comparable attenuation <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Pyasik et al., 2021)</ref>, as does the self-touch of an embodied prosthesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Fritsch et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These findings indicate that the processing of self-generated touch depends on learned relations between action and sensation.
The efference copy hypothesis implies that only the predicted sensation should be attenuated.

However, in rats, self-grooming was associated with widespread inhibition of somatosensory cortex and reduced responses to simultaneous external touch (Ishiyama et al., 2019); similarly in humans, self-touch leads to widespread cortical deactivations in functional imaging and can also reduce detection of additional tactile stimuli (Boehme et al., 2019).
text.formatted: However, in rats, self-grooming was associated with widespread inhibition of somatosensory cortex and reduced responses to simultaneous external touch <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Ishiyama et al., 2019)</ref>; similarly in humans, self-touch leads to widespread cortical deactivations in functional imaging and can also reduce detection of additional tactile stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Boehme et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In illusory self-touch, some deviations from a "perfect" prediction seem to be accepted by the nervous system (White et al., 2010) and that illusory alterations of body ownership or perturbation of trajectories do not always affect attenuation (Van Doorn et al., 2014; Van Doorn et al., 2015).
text.formatted: In illusory self-touch, some deviations from a "perfect" prediction seem to be accepted by the nervous system <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(White et al., 2010)</ref> and that illusory alterations of body ownership or perturbation of trajectories do not always affect attenuation <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(Van Doorn et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">Van Doorn et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: At odds with this is recent evidence showing spatially specific attenuation (Knoetsch & Zimmermann, 2021).
text.formatted: At odds with this is recent evidence showing spatially specific attenuation <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Knoetsch & Zimmermann, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: One possible explanation for these somewhat contradictory findings is that tolerance of sensory discrepancies could depend on the current estimated of certainty of sensory input and of internal model priors (Chancel & Ehrsson, 2023; D'Angelo et al., 2026).
text.formatted: One possible explanation for these somewhat contradictory findings is that tolerance of sensory discrepancies could depend on the current estimated of certainty of sensory input and of internal model priors <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Chancel & Ehrsson, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">D'Angelo et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In how far this accounts for differences between self-touch paradigms remains to be tested.
In any case, attenuation cannot always mean that self-touch disappears from experience or loses its behavioral relevance (Boehme & Olausson, 2022).
text.formatted: In any case, attenuation cannot always mean that self-touch disappears from experience or loses its behavioral relevance <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Boehme & Olausson, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Sexual self-touch provides a particularly clear illustration of the distinction between sensory attenuation and functional insignificance: genital self-stimulation evokes identifiable somatosensory responses and can culminate in orgasm involving sensory and reward-related networks (Komisaruk et al., 2011; Wise et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Sexual self-touch provides a particularly clear illustration of the distinction between sensory attenuation and functional insignificance: genital self-stimulation evokes identifiable somatosensory responses and can culminate in orgasm involving sensory and reward-related networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Komisaruk et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">Wise et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This article will focus on non-sexual self-touch behaviors.

We recently showed that the positive qualitative evaluations of such self-touches, i.e. their pleasantness, softness, and smoothness, depend on complex interactions between agency and predictability (Enmalm et al., 2026), supporting the idea that self-touch, while attenuated, is still perceived as a meaningful stimulus.
text.formatted: We recently showed that the positive qualitative evaluations of such self-touches, i.e. their pleasantness, softness, and smoothness, depend on complex interactions between agency and predictability <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Enmalm et al., 2026)</ref>, supporting the idea that self-touch, while attenuated, is still perceived as a meaningful stimulus.

text.text: Here, I propose that one function of recurrent self-touch is to help maintain a coherent bodily self-experience.
We previously suggested that self-touch may provide evidence for updating internal models of the body, potentially reducing uncertainty despite sensory attenuation (Boehme & Olausson, 2022).
text.formatted: We previously suggested that self-touch may provide evidence for updating internal models of the body, potentially reducing uncertainty despite sensory attenuation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Boehme & Olausson, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Building on this possibility, I hypothesize that predictable, controllable relations between action and sensation can provide ongoing evidence of the body as both a source of action and a locus of sensation.
I refer to actions serving this proposed function as self-confirming behaviors.
This does not imply that all self-touch serves self-maintenance, or that its effects can be reduced to a single process.
It means that self-touch offers a potential window into how bodily self-experience is actively sustained (Figure 1).
text.formatted: It means that self-touch offers a potential window into how bodily self-experience is actively sustained (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Contemporary cognitive science increasingly rejects the idea that selfhood arises from isolated brain activity.

Instead, recent work shows that self-experience depends on the continuous interplay of perception, emotion, bodily regulation, social interaction, and environmental engagement (Fotopoulou & Tsakiris, 2017; Seth & Tsakiris, 2018).
text.formatted: Instead, recent work shows that self-experience depends on the continuous interplay of perception, emotion, bodily regulation, social interaction, and environmental engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Fotopoulou & Tsakiris, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Seth & Tsakiris, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Yet despite this convergence on embodiment and relationality, a central conceptual tension remains: Is the self best understood as a model, a process, a pattern, or an illusion?

In this article, I will use the working hypothesis of bodily self-experience as an actively maintained organization continuously (re-)generated through processes that establish, confirm, and stabilize a distinction between self and other across neural, bodily, environmental, and social systems.
Importantly, this view implies that the self is relational, i.e. the organization of the self depends on its ongoing differentiation from not-self.

A water whirl provides an intuitive analogy for the process-oriented assumption underlying this hypothesis: the whirlpool as a recognizable pattern can persist even as the water constituting it changes.
Similarly, continuity of bodily self-experience may be supported by ongoing activity rather than by an unchanging bodily state.
The analogy is intended only to illustrate stability through change; it does not establish a mechanism of self-touch or require a particular position on the ontological status of the self.
The central arising question is how recurrent self-touch may contribute to maintaining self-other distinction (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The central arising question is how recurrent self-touch may contribute to maintaining self-other distinction (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: By generating predictable sensory consequences, such actions may provide repeated evidence of the body as a distinct locus of sensation and source of action.
This gives the process-oriented perspective a concrete behavioral focus: the contribution of self-touch to the continuity of bodily self-experience.
Self-touch may help sustain the experience of a coherent bodily self.
I use bodily selfmaintenance to describe the processes through which experience of the body as one's own, and of oneself as a source of action, remains coherent over time.

From this working perspective, bodily self-experience is not simply established once and then retained unchanged; its continuity may depend in part on recurrent interactions between action, bodily signals, and sensory feedback.
During self-touch, we produce the movement and feel the resulting sensation simultaneously, allowing the relationship between action and bodily percept to be examined directly.

Bodily ownership, agency, and self-other distinction refer to different aspects of bodily selfexperience: experiencing the body as one's own, experiencing oneself as initiating an action, and distinguishing self-generated from externally generated events.
Self-touch brings these aspects together as we move a part of our own body, produce contact, and feel its consequences on the body.
The proposed self-confirming function may involve all three, although a change in one does not necessarily imply a corresponding change in the others.
Experimental tests should therefore specify which aspect is being assessed.
My central hypothesis is that self-touch can contribute to this continuity by generating predictable and controllable relations between movement and sensation.
The correspondence between an action and its tactile and proprioceptive consequences may provide evidence that the acting and sensing body belong to the same organism.
In this view, attenuation follows from the match between predicted and actual sensory consequences: the sensation is attenuated because it confirms the expected outcome of one's own action.

This proposed contribution to bodily selfexperience is compatible with other functions of self-touch, including attentional and affective regulation -it does not have to explain every instance of the behavior.
What does self-touch add to movement alone?

Movement provides ongoing proprioceptive feedback, while self-touch also couples the act of touching with the sensation of being touched at the corresponding place and time (Schutz-Bosbach et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Movement provides ongoing proprioceptive feedback, while self-touch also couples the act of touching with the sensation of being touched at the corresponding place and time <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Schutz-Bosbach et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The contact produced by one part of the body is simultaneously received by another, providing a close correspondence between action and tactile feedback from both sides of the contact.
This additional correspondence may strengthen confirmation of the body as both acting and sensing.

Our findings show that brain activity during self-touch differs from that during touching an object (Boehme et al., 2019) and from touching while being touched (Enmalm et al., 2025), suggesting that its processing depends on more than the presence of movement and tactile input alone.
text.formatted: Our findings show that brain activity during self-touch differs from that during touching an object <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Boehme et al., 2019)</ref> and from touching while being touched <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Enmalm et al., 2025)</ref>, suggesting that its processing depends on more than the presence of movement and tactile input alone.

text.text: For self-touch, the relevant candidate mechanism is the recurrent action-feedback cycle: movement generates tactile and proprioceptive consequences, these are related to expectations about the action, and subsequent behavior can adjust the sensory feedback available or the internal predictive model.
The empirical question is whether this cycle helps sustain or restore bodily self-experience, beyond any effects on arousal or attention.

The hypothesis therefore directs attention to whether the predictability and controllability of self-touch matter for its effects on the bodily sense of self, particularly when bodily self-experience has been perturbed.

Using neuroimaging paradigms involving self-referential judgments, autobiographical reflection, and self-related stimuli, foundational studies identified cortical midline structures -including medial prefrontal cortex, anterior and posterior cingulate -that are consistently engaged during self-related processing (Northoff et al., 2006; Qin et al., 2020; Shin et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Using neuroimaging paradigms involving self-referential judgments, autobiographical reflection, and self-related stimuli, foundational studies identified cortical midline structures -including medial prefrontal cortex, anterior and posterior cingulate -that are consistently engaged during self-related processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Northoff et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Qin et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Shin et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: From the present perspective, these regions should not be interpreted as the neural location of the self, but as components of a distributed system that differentiates self-and non-self-related information (Açıl et al., 2026; Zapparoli et al., 2026).
text.formatted: From the present perspective, these regions should not be interpreted as the neural location of the self, but as components of a distributed system that differentiates self-and non-self-related information <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Açıl et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">Zapparoli et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Research on embodiment challenges the notion that the experience of a coherent sense of self can be understood solely in terms of brain-based self-referential cognition.

Experimental paradigms such as the rubber hand illusion, full-body ownership illusions, and manipulations of agency demonstrated that bodily self-experience can be experimentally altered through manipulating multisensory integration (Blanke et al., 2015; Ehrsson et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Experimental paradigms such as the rubber hand illusion, full-body ownership illusions, and manipulations of agency demonstrated that bodily self-experience can be experimentally altered through manipulating multisensory integration <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Blanke et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Ehrsson et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: These findings are mechanistically important because they show: When multisensory coupling is experimentally reorganized, the boundaries of the bodily self shift, indicating that the felt body is continuously maintained through sensorimotor integration and calibration.
Similarly, the discovery of a peripersonal space and its malleability show that the direct environment impacts the bodily self and its boundaries (Bogdanova et al., 2021; Grivaz et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Similarly, the discovery of a peripersonal space and its malleability show that the direct environment impacts the bodily self and its boundaries <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Bogdanova et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Grivaz et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, interoception, the perception of internal bodily states, is increasingly recognized as a core component of selfhood.

Interoceptive signals and affective aspects of touch engage the insula and related viscerosensory networks, linking bodily state to ongoing perceptual and regulatory processes (Craig, 2003; Damasio, 2003; McGlone et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Interoceptive signals and affective aspects of touch engage the insula and related viscerosensory networks, linking bodily state to ongoing perceptual and regulatory processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Craig, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Damasio, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">McGlone et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Allostatic accounts propose that the brain continuously predicts bodily demands and regulates physiological states accordingly (Theriault et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Allostatic accounts propose that the brain continuously predicts bodily demands and regulates physiological states accordingly <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Theriault et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Zhang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In this framework, the organism maintains itself by continuously predicting, detecting, and correcting deviations from viable bodily states.

Taken this one step further, Tallon-Baudry suggests that interoceptive signals do not merely inform the organism about bodily states, but provide an ongoing coordination mechanism that temporally binds distributed neural, sensory, and visceral processes into a coherent organismlevel organization (Tallon-Baudry et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Taken this one step further, Tallon-Baudry suggests that interoceptive signals do not merely inform the organism about bodily states, but provide an ongoing coordination mechanism that temporally binds distributed neural, sensory, and visceral processes into a coherent organismlevel organization <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">(Tallon-Baudry et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Interoception may also contribute to determining whether external sensory events are relevant to the self.
Recent work shows that cardiac-related neural activity can facilitate the encoding of the self-relevance of external stimuli (Loescher et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent work shows that cardiac-related neural activity can facilitate the encoding of the self-relevance of external stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Loescher et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that bodily signals do not merely provide background information about internal state, but they can help organize incoming sensory information according to its relation to the organism, thereby helping regulate the experiential boundary between the own body and the external world.

At the same time, touch, both from others and from oneself, has been shown repeatedly to impact autonomic processes, e.g. heartrate variability (Püschel et al., 2022; Triscoli et al., 2017), sympathetic-parasympathetic balance (Candia-Rivera, Boehme, et al., 2024; Candia-Rivera, de Vico Fallani, et al., 2024), and stress regulation (Ditzen et al., 2007; Dreisoerner et al., 2021; Eckstein et al., 2020).
text.formatted: At the same time, touch, both from others and from oneself, has been shown repeatedly to impact autonomic processes, e.g. heartrate variability <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Püschel et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Triscoli et al., 2017)</ref>, sympathetic-parasympathetic balance (Candia-Rivera, <ref type="bibr">Boehme, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Candia-Rivera, de Vico Fallani, et al., 2024)</ref>, and stress regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Ditzen et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Dreisoerner et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Eckstein et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, regulation is not exclusively individual.
Increasing evidence suggests that bodily regulation is fundamentally social, that it occurs in the form of co-regulation (Atzil & Barrett, 2017; Bastos et al., 2025; Fotopoulou & Tsakiris, 2017).
text.formatted: Increasing evidence suggests that bodily regulation is fundamentally social, that it occurs in the form of co-regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Atzil & Barrett, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bastos et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Fotopoulou & Tsakiris, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Human infants rely on caregivers for affective and physiological co-regulation, often mediated through touch (Ciaunica & Crucianelli, 2019).
text.formatted: Human infants rely on caregivers for affective and physiological co-regulation, often mediated through touch <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Ciaunica & Crucianelli, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Social interactions continue to influence autonomic regulation throughout adulthood (Gründahl et al., 2023; Riečanský et al., 2020; Sevi et al., 2022), contributing directly to allostasis.
text.formatted: Social interactions continue to influence autonomic regulation throughout adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Gründahl et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Riečanský et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Sevi et al., 2022)</ref>, contributing directly to allostasis.

text.text: From this perspective, social relationships become part of the regulatory architecture through which a bodily self-experience is maintained.
Accordingly, self-other distinction in a social context emerges from ongoing processes of mutual prediction, coordination, and differentiation.
Interindividual interactions continuously calibrate the boundaries through which a self remains distinct while remaining open to exchange.

This is supported by neuroscientific studies on interpersonal neural synchrony (Mayo & Shamay-Tsoory, 2024) and mutual neural predictions of interaction partners in humans (Wang et al., 2025) and in animals (Kingsbury et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This is supported by neuroscientific studies on interpersonal neural synchrony <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Mayo & Shamay-Tsoory, 2024)</ref> and mutual neural predictions of interaction partners in humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">(Wang et al., 2025)</ref> and in animals <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Kingsbury et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Intersubjectivity is therefore not added onto an already established self but participates in its constitution and maintenance.
Taken together, these findings situate bodily self-experience within ongoing interactions between sensory processing, bodily regulation, and social exchange.
Self-touch brings several of these processes together in a single action: we generate a movement, predict its sensory consequences, and feel the resulting contact on our own body.

The correspondence between prediction and sensation may repeatedly confirm the body as both the source and the recipient of an actionand thereby also differentiate it from the non-self, specifically from tactile sensation arising from touching the surrounding world and social touch from others.
This raises the possibility that everyday self-touch contributes to the continuity of bodily self-experience, linking its familiar regulatory functions to the maintenance of self-other distinction.
As discussed, contemporary accounts of selfhood emphasize the role of interoception and predictive processing.
However, comparatively less attention has been paid to the unique role of touch in the constitution and maintenance of the experience of the bodily self.
This omission is surprising, as touch occupies a privileged position at the boundary between self and world (Boehme, 2025b).
text.formatted: This omission is surprising, as touch occupies a privileged position at the boundary between self and world <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Boehme, 2025b)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike vision or audition, touch is inherently reciprocal: to touch is always to simultaneously be touched (Boehme, 2025b; Legrand, 2006).
text.formatted: Unlike vision or audition, touch is inherently reciprocal: to touch is always to simultaneously be touched <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Boehme, 2025b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Legrand, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: As such, tactile experience directly engages the distinction between self and non-self while at the same time revealing their continuous interaction (Boehme, 2025b; Boehme et al., 2019; Boehme & Olausson, 2022).
text.formatted: As such, tactile experience directly engages the distinction between self and non-self while at the same time revealing their continuous interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Boehme, 2025b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Boehme et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Boehme & Olausson, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, touch is not merely a sensory contribution to the experience of the body.
It is one of the key constitutive mechanisms through which a coherent bodily self-experience is maintained.
The importance of touch becomes apparent when considering the development of the bodily self representation (Cascio, 2010).
text.formatted: The importance of touch becomes apparent when considering the development of the bodily self representation <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Cascio, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: From the earliest stages of life, tactile interactions with caregivers contribute to physiological regulation, affective development, and the establishment of bodily boundaries (Ciaunica & Crucianelli, 2019; Croy et al., 2022).

text.text: The human experience of their sense of self does not emerge in isolation but develops through repeated cycles of bodily interaction and co-regulation, first during pregnancy only with the body of the mother, later also with other bodies of caregivers (Ciaunica, Constant, et al., 2021; Ciaunica & Crucianelli, 2019).

text.text: Importantly, these effects extend beyond the transmission of sensory information.

However, it has to be considered that the patients suffered from sensory alterations in the affected limb, which might evoke prediction errors in the close action-prediction-loop of self-touch -therefore this finding can be interpreted as support for the here suggested mechanism, i.e. in this clinical case, the self-touch did not evoke the predicted sensations and therefore did not strengthen ownership.

From the perspective developed here, touch is significant not only because it provides passive or circumstantial information about self-other-differentiation (Boehme et al., 2019), but especially because it allows the individual to actively constitute, probe, and confirm the self (Boehme, 2025b).

Crossing the hands strengthened subjective illusory self-touch during synchronous stimulation without increasing proprioceptive drift (Pozeg et al., 2014), while large angular misalignment could diminish the illusion even when the prosthetic hand remained anatomically plausible (White et al., 2015).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that the experience of self-touch depends on the integration of tactile and proprioceptive information within spatial and anatomical constraints, rather than on sensory synchrony alone.

Autistic people show substantial heterogeneity in sensory processing, interoception, and social experience (Bolis et al., 2018; Cascio, 2010; Garfinkel et al., 2016; Kimber et al., 2024), indicating potential differences in how autistic individuals maintain their sense of self (Russo et al., 2025).

text.text: Behaviors such as stimming, self-touch, and repetitive sensory engagement can, in this view, be reconceived -not as epiphenomenal symptoms, but as active self-confirmation strategies that stabilize the sense of self.
Importantly, this does not imply a deficient sense of self.
On the contrary, the self-experience may become more salient precisely because its boundaries require more active maintenance and negotiation (Ciaunica, Roepstorff, et al., 2021).

text.text: The body may appear less transparent and more continuously present within experience.

This perspective offers a novel interpretation of stimming behaviors: Repetitive sensory behaviors are typically understood in terms of arousal regulation, sensory modulation, or predictive stabilization (Baranek et al., 1997; Russo et al., 2025).

text.text: While these functions are important, stimming may also serve a more fundamental role: that of active self-maintenance.

Repetitive tactile, proprioceptive, vestibular, or auditory stimulation generates highly predictable, reliable, and controllable sensory feedback that provides evidence for the bodily self-model and supports self-other distinction, particularly under conditions of uncertainty, overstimulation, or interpersonal overwhelm.
Importantly, stimming is often described not only as distress-reducing but as pleasurable, grounding, joyful, or organizing (Kapp et al., 2019; Morris et al., 2025; Pfuhl & Ekblad, 2025).

text.text: In self-touch, the correspondence between self-generated movement and familiar bodily sensations may contribute to this grounding experience.
This suggests that repetitive sensory engagement may be intrinsically reinforcing because of its key function of predictable and controllable bodily feedback -also in neurotypical individuals.
Within the present hypothesis, this correspondence provides repeated confirmation of the body as a source of action and sensation, helping sustain a coherent bodily self-experience.

Exploring when autistic individuals seek self-touch, and which aspects of the resulting feedback they find grounding or pleasurable, could help clarify how this proposed function relates to sensory and emotional regulation.
At the same time, it is important not to treat autistic experiences as homogeneous (Cheong et al., 2025).

text.text: The present proposal should therefore be understood not as a generalization but as a theoretical framework for exploring how different forms of sensory and bodily percepts may emerge through different modes of self-world regulation.
More broadly, neurodivergent lived experience may offer a particularly valuable perspective on the nature of bodily self-experience.

Because many neurotypical individuals experience the body as relatively transparent during everyday life, the active processes through which it is maintained often remain implicit (Ciaunica, Roepstorff, et al., 2021).

text.text: In this sense, neurodivergent forms of embodiment may provide not merely clinical deviations from a norm, but important phenomenological insights into the biological and relational foundations of subjectivity.
Schizophrenia provides a different case in which self-maintenance has become unstable.

text.text: Within the present framework, such beliefs can be understood as attempts to restore coherence when lower-level processes supporting self-other distinction become unreliable.

Thus, when the basic bodily distinction becomes unstable (e.g., "this is my hand touching me"), higher-order inference may provide an alternative explanation (e.g., "a demon is touching me and controlling my actions" -paraphrased citation from a patient commenting on the relevance of our research).

This raises the possibility that restoring reliable self-generated sensory feedback could help re-stabilize the underlying selfmaintaining organization, although whether behaviors such as self-touch can do so remains an empirical question.
The framework yields three predictions.
Experimentally destabilizing bodily ownership, agency, or self-location should increase behaviors that generate reliable self-produced sensory evidence, relative to a matched control condition.
Opportunities for movement and touch should be equivalent, and arousal and cognitive demand should be measured or controlled.
No selective increase despite verified destabilization would challenge this behavioral prediction.

Following destabilization, access to contingent self-generated tactile feedback should accelerate recovery of the prespecified bodily-self measure compared with matched movement without touch, passive or externally generated feedback, and a no-feedback condition.
Recovery should be assessed repeatedly rather than inferred from a single post-intervention rating.
Equivalent recovery across active and matched passive conditions would weaken the claim that active generation has a distinctive restorative contribution.

Introducing unpredictable delays or spatial mismatches into the consequences of self-touch should eliminate the additional recovery benefit of reliable contingent feedback, while preserving the amount of stimulation and motor activity.
If restoration remains unchanged despite a verified disruption of perceived predictability or contingency, the proposed mechanism would be challenged.
Convergent support would require changes in bodily-self outcomes that cannot be explained solely by reduced distress, increased attention, or generic sensory stimulation.
The initial experimental scope is self-touch, with extension to other behaviors requiring separate evidence.
Why do we touch ourselves?
Alongside its roles in sensory, emotional, and cognitive regulation, self-touch may help sustain a coherent bodily self-experience.

I propose that the predictable relation between movement and its tactile and proprioceptive consequences provides repeated confirmation of the body as both a source of action and a locus of sensation.
Within this account, sensory attenuation follows from successful prediction: the sensory consequences confirm the expected outcome of one's own action.
Recurrent self-touch may thus contribute to the ongoing maintenance of bodily agency, ownership, and self-other distinction.

The cases of autism and psychosis raise questions about how this contribution may vary with altered sensory experience and dysfunctional action-prediction-loops. interpretation, and ideas are the author's original contributions.
